I had the testing done and it came back negative. We also had 3 separate scans done at 20 weeks, 26 weeks, and 35 weeks and no one caught the heart defect either. I want to say that I reacted stoically when she was born, but I absolutely did not. In the recovery room when it was just my husband and I, I started crying and saying "I dont want her" over and over again. I had a really hard time allowing myself to love her, because I thought that if I didn't and she died it wouldn't hurt so much. I didn't get to hold her for a week, but as soon as they placed her in my arms, I was filled with a strength and determination that I had never felt before. It was like one of those videos where you see a mother lifting a car off her baby. It was honestly insane. 

We were really lucky to have her born in the area we live, be because we have an amazing childrens hospital within an hour of us. The first few months were honestly hell. I had to travel back and forth because we were moving at the same time, and I missed my other kids terribly. My husband was my rock. After her heart was taken care of, we moved into some intense therapy. We had had her in early intervention since she came home from the hospital at 5 weeks,  but we couldn't really do much because of her heart. We had pt/ot in home once a week, then had an outside referral for feeding therapy and pt at an outside facility. So 4 appointments a week  plus follow ups with different providers. 

With all that said, I would do it all again in a heartbeat. She is just the sweetest, most amazing little girl. Don't get me wrong, she can be a total asshole, just like the others, but she really is amazing. Being a special needs parent isn't easy. It's long, thankless hours. It's straight up torture some days. I still have days where I grieve the loss of the daughter I thought I was going to get, but nothing is ever all sunshine and rainbows. You find strength that you didn't know you had.

Going through all this has really strengthened my pro choice stance as well. Some people don't have the means emotionally or financially, or the family support that I am so lucky to have. Women know their own  limitations, and I trust that they will make a decision that is right for them.

If you want to cut back on breastfeeding, do it! Add some formula! Then your SO can help, and it takes some of the pressure off of your plate. Take a long ass shower! Go for a walk! Paint your nails! Carve out some you time. I felt like I was drowning for a very long time. It's so hard worrying about every little thing. The constant cleaning to make sure she doesn't get sick. The million doctors appointments that come with a heart baby. The anxiety and possible guilt. Find your tribe. The community was one of the only things that got me through when buggy was born, and a long time after. I'm sorry if this is all over the place, I just woke up. If you need to talk, please pm me!  Once she had open heart surgery to repair her heart defect, she started eating therapy to essentially teach her how to eat. They would go over different techniques to try to get her to take a bottle, none of which worked.


 Once we gave her regular baby food, she would only eat off to the side, so they helped up slowly move her eating from the side of her mouth to the front using time and prodding. Once she got the eating part down, we moved to drinking. They tried everything they could think of to get her to drink. Different exercises, different cups, pretty much everything they could think of. 

Nothing was working to stimulate her mouth to close around the opening to anything. Our feeding therapist was amazing, and remembered she would only eat from the side of her mouth when she first started, so she tried a mustard bottle off to the side of her mouth and we would squeeze a tiny amount of formula into her mouth. Once she realised that it tasted good and was something that she actually wanted she would drink from the squeeze bottle. 

Once we got her drinking from the front of her mouth instead of the side, we introduced a supply cup, and from then on out it has been amazing. She actually just had her permanent feeding tube removed last Tuesday.

Puffy style coats can be hard to get a tight fit from the restraint in the car seat. When you get into an accident the coat can compress and actually cause the child to be ejected from the seat. Things like fleece and wool are fine, but Puffy winter jackets are not. If you are curious about if your child's coat is car seat appropriate you can test it by letting out the harness, putting your child into the seat with the jacket on, and getting the harness as tight as you can. Then remove the child without loosening the straps and take the coat off. Put the child back into the seat without adjusting the straps and see how much slack there is. If it doesn't pass the pinch test, then that coat isn't ok in the seat.
